stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Explore the solar system schematic. Drag the time slider to watch planets revolve at their real relative rates. Toggle log-scaled radii to see the outer planets, and toggle the seasons view to see Earth's axial tilt shift the subsolar point. Advance once you've tried all three: scrub time, swap the scale, and open seasons.
stages.concept: The Solar System has eight planets orbiting the Sun. Inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and close; outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are large and far. Distances span orders of magnitude — Neptune is $\sim 30$ AU from the Sun (1 AU = Earth–Sun distance). Earth spins on a tilted axis ($\sim 23.5°$) as it orbits: the tilt, not the distance, causes the seasons. The Sun itself is one of $\sim 10^{11}$ stars in the Milky Way galaxy.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: The diagram is gone. Answer 5 questions in a row about scale, seasons, day/night, sizes, and our place in the galaxy. One wrong answer restarts the deck.
stages.concept: Order-of-magnitude astronomy: distances in AU inside the Solar System, in light-years for stars, in kiloparsecs for galactic scale. Seasons come from axial tilt; day and night come from Earth's rotation. The Sun is one ordinary star among hundreds of billions in the Milky Way — a spiral galaxy roughly $10^5$ ly across.

labels.question: question
labels.tip1: try the sliders and toggles above — coverage advances as you explore each control
labels.tip2: no diagram this stage — think first, then commit; a wrong answer resets the deck
labels.q_distance_prompt: Roughly how far is Neptune from the Sun, in astronomical units (AU)?
labels.q_seasons_a: The Earth-Sun distance changes a lot during the year.
labels.q_seasons_b: The Sun's brightness changes during the year.
labels.q_seasons_c: Earth's rotation axis is tilted relative to its orbital plane.
labels.q_seasons_d: The Moon blocks part of the sunlight seasonally.
labels.q_daynight_prompt: What causes the alternation of day and night at a given place on Earth?
labels.q_daynight_b: Earth's rotation about its own axis.
labels.q_size_prompt: Which ordering of diameters is correct?
labels.q_galaxy_prompt: Where is our Solar System located within the Milky Way?
labels.q_galaxy_a: At the exact center of the galaxy.
labels.q_galaxy_b: On one of the spiral arms, far from the galactic center.
labels.q_galaxy_c: In a small satellite galaxy orbiting the Milky Way.
labels.q_galaxy_d: Between two neighboring galaxies, outside any spiral arm.

1.1: There are three controls on the right: a time slider, a scale toggle, and a seasons toggle. Try each one.
1.2: Scrub time and watch the inner planets lap the outer ones. Then flip 'linear' to 'log' to squeeze Neptune into view.
1.3: Turn on 'seasons' to see Earth's tilted axis and the subsolar point drift between the tropics as time advances.

2.1: Think first, then answer. Order-of-magnitude reasoning: is Neptune closer to 1, 10, or 100 AU?
2.2: Seasons: what changes between June and December — the distance, or the angle of sunlight? Day/night: what changes over 24 hours — the orbit, or the spin?
2.3: Sizes: Sun ≫ Jupiter > Earth > Moon (roughly ten times each step). Milky Way: we sit on a spiral arm, well off-center.
